# Results — Study 715 ("Vinyl is back — a trend to trade?")

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Is the vinyl revival a trend
you can trade? We test the strongest tradable version: the **RIAA U.S. vinyl-revenue
series** (hardcoded, cited, **approximate** — a labelled proxy for the trend, not a live
feed or a price) and the only **listed** ways to buy the trade (Warner Music `WMG`,
Spotify `SPOT`, Universal `UMG.AS`), each benchmarked against `SPY`. Offline &
deterministic; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Vinyl-revenue index | **Hardcoded, cited, approximate** RIAA year-end U.S. vinyl LP/EP retail value ($M), base 100 @ 2010-12-31 — see [`docs/references.md`](references.md). **A PROXY for the trend, not a price.** |
| Equity proxies | `WMG` (Warner Music, NASDAQ) · `SPOT` (Spotify, NYSE) · `UMG.AS` (Universal Music, Euronext AMS) — month-end Adj Close via yfinance, cached under `_cache/` |
| Benchmark | `SPY` (month-end Adj Close, yfinance) |
| As-of | 2025-12-31 (month-end; no partial-year bar) |
| Vinyl window | 2010 → 2024 (RIAA year-end levels; 2024 is the latest full-year report) |
| Equity window | 2018-04 → 2025-12 (SPOT from its 2018-04 listing: 92 monthly returns; WMG from 2020-06: 66; UMG.AS from 2021-09: 51) |

> **Why a proxy, stated as a decision.** The RIAA revenue database is a public web app,
> **not a freely-pullable API**, and — more important — vinyl *revenue* is not a security.
> Rather than dress industry revenue up as a tradable price we (a) hardcode a small,
> clearly-cited, **approximate** annual series whose *shape* — an 18-year climb, CDs
> overtaken in revenue (2020) and units (2022), past $1B (2021) to ~$1.4B (2024) — is the
> load-bearing public fact, and (b) test the **tradable** equity proxies a public investor
> can actually buy. A label's or a streamer's equity is **not** a stack of records; they
> are labelled proxies throughout.

## Half 1 — did the vinyl TREND out-grow the S&P? (revenue index vs SPY)

The (approximate, cited) RIAA vinyl revenue, year-end $M and base-100 index:

| year | 2010 | 2014 | 2018 | 2019 | 2020 | 2021 | 2022 | 2023 | 2024 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| revenue $M | 89 | 321 | 419 | 479 | **643** | **1003** | 1225 | 1353 | 1400 |
| YoY | — | +52% | +6% | +14% | **+34%** | **+56%** | +22% | +10% | +4% |

Headline risk/return of the revenue index vs SPY:

| series | CAGR | ann. vol | Sharpe | max drawdown |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Vinyl revenue index** (2010–2024) | **+21.75%** | 19.5% | 1.19 | **−8.1%** |
| SPY (year-end, 2018–2025) | +17.18% | 16.9% | — | −18.2% |

**The trend genuinely out-grew stocks** — vinyl *revenue* compounded ~22%/yr vs SPY's
~17%. But that is the trap: **revenue growth is not an investable return.** There is no
security that pays out the RIAA series. On the 6 overlapping years the mean annual excess
(revenue growth − SPY) is **+4.9%/yr, t = +0.46** (p = 0.67, n = 6) — a real trend, but
not even a *statistically clean* growth win, and in any case one you **cannot buy**.

## Half 2 — the tradable proxies vs SPY (the only thing you can buy)

Monthly Adj Close, Newey-West (6-lag) alpha vs SPY. **These are labelled proxies.**

| series | CAGR | ann. vol | Sharpe | max DD | alpha/yr | beta | NW *t*(α) | p |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **WMG** (Warner Music) | +2.76% | 36.4% | 0.25 | **−52.2%** | −11.5% | 1.24 | −1.23 | 0.22 |
| **SPOT** (Spotify) | +18.14% | **46.8%** | 0.58 | **−74.9%** | +2.0% | 1.65 | +0.12 | 0.91 |
| **UMG.AS** (Universal) | +1.30% | 27.3% | 0.18 | −24.2% | −6.4% | 0.85 | −0.66 | 0.51 |
| SPY | +13.59% | 16.5% | **0.86** | −23.9% | — | — | — | — |

**No proxy shows a significant alpha vs SPY** (|t| < 1.3 for all three). Two of the three
*badly lagged* the index — Warner (+2.8%/yr) and Universal (+1.3%/yr) delivered a fraction
of SPY's +13.6% with far deeper drawdowns. The one that *beat* SPY, Spotify (+18.1%), did
it on **streaming**, not vinyl — β≈1.65, a −75% round-trip, and an alpha of +2%/yr that is
statistically zero (*t* = +0.12). **There is no harvestable "vinyl" edge in anything you
can buy.**

## Half 3 — the collector carry haircut (what owning the trend really costs)

You can't buy the revenue series, so the only *direct* way to hold the trend is to buy and
sell physical records. That round-trip pays a marketplace-fee + condition-discount spread
(~**30%**) over a ~**5-year** hold, plus ~**1%/yr** storage carry:

| case | gross | net after spread + carry |
|---|--:|--:|
| **charitable** — records appreciate at the full revenue-growth rate | +21.75%/yr | **+12.23%/yr** |
| **realistic** — per-record resale ≈ flat (reissues expand supply) | +0.00%/yr | **−7.82%/yr** |

The charitable case is a fantasy: a *revived* market **presses more records**, so your copy
does not appreciate at the industry's revenue-growth rate — new supply meets the demand.
On the realistic read (flat per-record resale), the collector's net return is **negative**
once the spread and storage are charged. Either way, the ~22%/yr revenue growth is not
something a flipper keeps.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful

A deterministic, fixed-seed "revival" path (planted CAGR +20%, σ = 4%/mo, seed 715): the
inference engine recovers the planted up-sign and a finite Sharpe — peak ≈ 596 → end ≈ 558,
recovered CAGR **+18.9%**, Sharpe 1.28, max DD −15.3%, `sign_ok = 1`. The harness can bank
a planted signal, so the null on the real proxies is a real null, not a broken pipeline.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The vinyl *trend* is real (revenue +21.8%/yr, 18 straight years), but
  revenue growth is not an investable return, and the annual-excess growth win isn't even
  clean (*t* = +0.46). What you can actually *buy* shows **no significant alpha**: WMG
  *t* = −1.23, SPOT *t* = +0.12, UMG.AS *t* = −0.66 — none clears |t| ≥ 2 in the trade's
  favour. There is no tradable vinyl edge.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** You cannot custody the RIAA series. Two of three listed proxies
  *lagged* SPY badly (WMG +2.8%, UMG +1.3% vs +13.6%) with deeper drawdowns; the one that
  beat it (SPOT) is high-β streaming beta with a −75% drawdown and zero alpha; and
  physically flipping records nets **negative** once a revived (supply-expanding) market
  meets the marketplace spread + storage carry.
- **Already priced in? — CONFIRMED.** Vinyl is ~7% of a business ~84% driven by streaming;
  the majors are priced on streaming, and no tradable proxy carries a vinyl-attributable
  premium. Whatever the revival is worth is already in the tape — or, more precisely, too
  small to move it. A famous, public, 18-year trend is not a secret you can trade.

> **Caveat (named, not buried).** The revenue index here is a **small, hardcoded,
> approximate** reconstruction of public RIAA reporting — its *shape* is defensible but its
> precise year-end values are not a live feed, and it is *industry revenue*, not a price.
> The equity proxies are exactly that — labelled proxies for "owning the trade," not a
> stack of records, and their returns are dominated by streaming. Both limitations push the
> verdict toward humility: the revival is real, but nothing here is a tradable edge, and
> several lines say the opposite.
